addressed_problems.content: The paper observes that lottery tickets found on the Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) set can sometimes outperform vanilla lottery tickets at very high sparsity levels, suggesting an additional regularization effect from training on a reduced set of challenging examples. However, the theoretical mechanism underlying this improved generalization is not explained, and the authors explicitly leave its investigation for future work.

While the paper demonstrates that PrAC sets are transferable across different network architectures on the same dataset, potentially amortizing the cost of constructing the PrAC set, no formal analysis is provided to quantify the trade-off between the initial construction cost and the amortized savings when applying the PrAC set to multiple target models. Determining when this cost is justified, especially for very large target models or datasets, remains an unresolved issue.

The effectiveness of the PrAC framework depends on several hyperparameters, including the forgetting threshold (ℰ_F) for selecting critical examples, the number of training epochs used to collect forgetting statistics, and the Hamming-distance threshold for early stopping. As shown in Table A4, varying these values affects both the size of the PrAC set and the final accuracy of the found subnetworks. The paper does not provide optimal, generally-applicable settings or adaptive selection strategies for these hyperparameters, leaving this as an open challenge.

The evaluation of the PrAC co-design framework is limited to image classification tasks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet) and network architectures from the ResNet and VGG families. It remains unknown whether the approach generalizes to other modalities (e.g., text, audio), different tasks (e.g., object detection, semantic segmentation, natural language processing), or larger-scale datasets. The paper explicitly identifies this as a direction for future work.

Deep neural networks are heavily over-parameterized and practitioners therefore use pruning to obtain compact inference models; however, the end-to-end process of locating sparse, trainable subnetworks (the "lottery ticket" winning tickets) relies on Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) or similar train-prune-retrain cycles that are computationally burdensome. Prior attempts to avoid costly IMP have followed two orthogonal directions: (a) finding data-level "coresets" or active-learning subsets that reduce training cost but are designed to preserve generalization for dense models, and (b) finding sparse subnetworks at initialization or early training (e.g., SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow) that avoid heavy retraining but typically produce subnetworks with clearly inferior performance to IMP-found tickets. What is lacking is a principled way to co-design data selection and model pruning so that (i) the selected training subset encodes not only the dense-model generalization but also the sparse-model trainability, and (ii) finding winning tickets becomes practically efficient on realistic datasets and architectures. Because existing coreset methods do not target the harder objective of producing sparse-trainable subnetworks, and pruning-at-initialization methods trade correctness for efficiency, practitioners have no method that both substantially reduces the computational cost of ticket-finding and preserves (or improves) the final sparse-subnetwork accuracy on common vision benchmarks. This deficiency prevents scaling lottery-ticket discovery to larger datasets/models, obstructs amortization of the ticket-finding cost, and leaves open whether data-level sparsity can materially accelerate and/or improve model-level sparsity discovery.

nodes.content: In the context of finding trainable sparse subnetworks (the lottery ticket problem), existing "coreset" or active-selection methods select examples that allow dense models to generalize but do not necessarily preserve the examples that are critical for identifying sparse, trainable connectivity patterns. Meanwhile, pruning disproportionately degrades performance on semantically ambiguous or underrepresented images, so a data subset suitable for dense training can omit examples that are pivotal for sparse-model trainability. Therefore, a selection criterion that explicitly targets samples that are both difficult to learn and sensitive to pruning is required: without such pruning-aware selection, any reduced dataset risks omitting the examples that determine which subnetworks will remain trainable after pruning, and thus cannot reliably produce winning tickets via reduced-data IMP.

Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) finds high-quality winning tickets but requires repeated full-data training iterations and repeated pruning, making it computationally expensive on practical datasets. A pipeline that replaces full-data training at each pruning iteration with training on a carefully constructed, much smaller dataset would reduce per-epoch cost and can potentially reduce required epochs per iteration, but such a pipeline must ensure the selected subset preserves the signals necessary to (a) locate trainable sparse masks and (b) avoid pruning-induced forgetting. The proposed iterative co-design operationalizes this idea by embedding PrAC construction inside the IMP-style loop so the data subset evolves jointly with the mask, addressing the absence of a practical, integrated method that targets both data- and model-level sparsity for efficient lottery ticket discovery.

Even if a smaller PrAC set reduces per-epoch cost linearly, additional speedups require reducing the number of epochs/iterations because fewer and easier-to-fit examples can lead to faster convergence. A simple proportional scaling of iterations and a principled early-stopping rule tied to mask stability are necessary to realize non-linear gains in total training effort. Without such measures, the mere reduction in dataset size would not necessarily translate into the observed large decreases in total training iterations needed to find a matching subnetwork.

Quantifying achievable data reduction is necessary to evaluate practical efficiency: prior coreset and dataset-distillation approaches report compact subsets for dense-model training, but it was unknown how compact a pruning-aware subset must be to support lottery-ticket discovery. The size ranges above provide concrete, empirical bounds on how much data can be removed while still maintaining the ability to find high-quality sparse subnetworks; without these measurements one cannot assess whether pruning-aware data reduction yields meaningful wall-clock or computational savings in practice.

The central practical gap is that vanilla IMP achieves high-quality winning tickets but at excessive computational cost; it was unknown whether a co-designed, pruning-aware subset could preserve winning-ticket quality while producing substantial iteration savings. Demonstrating concrete iteration savings quantifies the potential practical benefits and shows that PrAC-driven ticket finding can materially reduce the wall-clock and computational resources required to locate matching subnetworks.

A concern with any reduced-data approach is that it may degrade the final sparse model's accuracy compared to full-data IMP. Establishing whether PrAC-driven pruning preserves or improves final performance is essential to justify the efficiency trade-off. Observing parity (or gains) in accuracy across sparsity levels demonstrates that PrAC selection can be a viable alternative to full-data IMP without accuracy sacrifice, addressing the worry that data reduction must necessarily come at the cost of final performance.

Constructing a PrAC set requires additional computation relative to naive random sampling; for the idea to be practical one must be able to amortize that cost. If a PrAC set discovered with a small/cheap architecture can be reused to find tickets in larger/expensive architectures on the same dataset, the initial overhead is shared, and the approach becomes practically attractive for large-model settings. Without transferability across architectures, the extra cost of constructing PrAC sets could negate efficiency gains when applied to large target models.

Alternatives to IMP either reduce data (coresets/active learning) or avoid retraining (pruning at initialization), but prior comparisons did not evaluate a co-designed approach that explicitly targets pruning fragility while keeping identical computation budgets. Establishing superiority over these baselines under matched resources is necessary to demonstrate that the gains arise from the pruning-aware data selection rather than from extra computation; otherwise, any reported improvements could be artefacts of unequal training budgets.

It was unclear whether training-difficulty signals alone (forgetting statistics) would suffice to preserve pruning robustness or whether examples uniquely fragile to pruning must be included. Understanding the individual contributions of CET and CEP informs whether a single selection criterion is adequate or a union is needed. Without this ablation, one could not justify the additional step of adding pruning-disagreement samples into the PrAC set.

To provide intuition why pruning-aware subsets preserve sparse-model trainability, it is necessary to characterize which examples are retained. If PrAC selection simply picked a class-imbalanced or trivial subset, performance parity could be accidental or fragile. Demonstrating that PrAC contains harder, ambiguous examples but remains class-balanced supports the hypothesis that PrAC preserves the critical, informative inputs that determine sparse-model behavior, and explains empirically why PrAC tickets generalize.

A Pruning-Aware Critical set (PrAC set) is a compact subset of the full training data $\mathcal{D}_0$ constructed to capture examples that are both (i) hard-to-memorize during model training and (ii) easy-to-forget by the model after pruning. Concretely, the construction uses two selection criteria: (A) forgetting statistics per sample (the number of transitions from correct to incorrect classification during training), and (B) prediction disagreement between the full dense model $f(\boldsymbol{\theta},x)$ and a pruned subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},x)$, where a sample is included if its forgetting count exceeds a threshold $\mathcal{E}_\text{F}$ or if the two models predict different classes. The PrAC set $\mathcal{P}$ is the union of the examples selected by (A) and (B), and is intended to encode both dense-model generalization difficulty and pruning-induced fragility.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 1 is definitional: it proposes the PrAC set construction criterion (forgetting statistics + prediction disagreement). No load-bearing weak points or highlights were identified, because the definition itself is not an empirical claim requiring probabilistic assessment. The derivation is straightforward and no uncertain bridges are present in the description of the criterion; its effectiveness is tested in later conclusions.

nodes.title: Definition and construction criterion of the Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) set

nodes.content: An iterative co-design pipeline alternates between (i) constructing a PrAC set and (ii) pruning the current network to update a binary mask $\boldsymbol{m}\in\{0,1\}^{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\|_0}$, where $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ are the initial network parameters, yielding a matching subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},\cdot)$. The pipeline initializes with $\boldsymbol{m}=\mathbf{1}$ and the working training set $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_0$, the full training data, then in each iteration: train $f(\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_0,\cdot)$ on $\mathcal{D}$ for $T$ epochs while recording forgetting statistics; add samples with forgetting count greater than the threshold $\mathcal{E}_\text{F}$ to the PrAC set $\mathcal{P}$; prune a fraction $\rho$ of remaining weights from the trained subnetwork and update $\boldsymbol{m}$; add to $\mathcal{P}$ those training examples on which the full and pruned models disagree in prediction; set $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{P}$ and repeat until the desired overall sparsity $s$ is reached. The output is a sparse mask $\boldsymbol{m}$ and its PrAC set $\mathcal{P}$.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 describes the iterative co-design pipeline (Algorithm 1) as a procedural framework. No load-bearing weak points or highlights were identified; the pipeline is an algorithmic specification whose effectiveness is empirically assessed in subsequent conclusions. The description is internally consistent and does not rely on uncertain assumptions beyond those tested elsewhere.

nodes.title: Iterative data-model co-design pipeline to find sparse masks using PrAC sets

nodes.content: Two practical training strategies are introduced for turning a PrAC set $\mathcal{P}$ into concrete training savings: (i) dynamic training-iteration scaling using the formula $N = \frac{|\mathcal{P}|}{|\mathcal{D}_0|} N_0$, where $\mathcal{D}_0$ is the full training dataset, $N_0$ is the number of training iterations used when training on $\mathcal{D}_0$, and $|\mathcal{P}|$ is the size of the PrAC set; and (ii) early stopping based on mask convergence monitored by Hamming distance between successive binary masks, with a default Hamming-threshold of $0.07$ used to interrupt training early and proceed to pruning. The Hamming distances between masks empirically converge early in training (around half of the full training iterations), validating the early-stopping mechanism.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 3's claim that dynamic iteration scaling and early stopping yield practical training savings is partially supported. The linear scaling assumption (P1) is a load-bearing risk: if false, the savings could be overestimated and the subnetworks undertrained, and no highlight addresses this risk directly. The early stopping threshold (P2) is a secondary risk, but highlight H1 partially insulates it by providing measured convergence of Hamming distances, showing that the mechanism is grounded in observation rather than arbitrary. The overall credibility of the savings figures hinges on the unvalidated scaling rule, which remains the dominant vulnerability.

nodes.title: Training-efficiency techniques for PrAC-based ticket finding: dynamic iteration scaling and early stopping

nodes.content: On standard image-classification benchmarks, the Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) sets identified by the iterative data-model co-design algorithm (which alternates between constructing a PrAC set and pruning the network to update the mask) are substantially smaller than the full training sets and vary with task complexity: CIFAR-10 PrAC sizes range from 35.32% to 37.07% of the training set, CIFAR-100 PrAC sizes range from 69.55% to 78.19%, and Tiny-ImageNet PrAC sizes range from 68.23% to 75.10% of their respective training sets.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4 reports specific PrAC set size ranges across benchmarks. Premise P3 shows that these sizes are contingent on the forgetting threshold E_F=0, and that larger thresholds reduce both size and performance, making the reported numbers not robust as intrinsic dataset properties. No highlight offsets this uncertainty. The conclusion's quantitative estimates of data reduction are therefore not reliable as general characterizations, and the prior probability reflects this fragility.

nodes.title: Observed PrAC set sizes on standard vision benchmarks

nodes.content: Using Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) sets within the iterative data-model co-design pipeline (which alternates between constructing a PrAC set and pruning) and applying dynamic iteration scaling (linearly scaling training iterations with PrAC set size) and early stopping (based on Hamming distance convergence of binary masks) yields large empirical reductions in the total training iterations needed to find matching subnetworks (subnetworks that can be trained to achieve comparable accuracy to the full dense network): on CIFAR-10 the pipeline achieves training-iteration savings in the range 82.85%–92.77% (across architectures), on CIFAR-100 savings of 63.54%–74.92%, and on Tiny-ImageNet savings of 76.14%–86.56%, while producing subnetworks with test accuracies that match those found by standard Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP)-based "vanilla lottery ticket" procedures.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 5 claims large iteration savings while matching vanilla LT performance. The iteration savings are directly measured, but the matching criterion of one standard deviation (P4) introduces a methodological weak point: if a stricter equivalence standard were applied, some configurations might not match, reducing the savings that can be claimed. No highlight substantiates the criterion. The savings figures are credible only under the paper's own relaxed definition of matching, which limits the conclusion's strength.

nodes.title: Large reductions in ticket-finding training iterations while matching vanilla LT performance

nodes.content: Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC)-found subnetworks ("PrAC lottery tickets") achieve test accuracies that are statistically indistinguishable from vanilla lottery tickets found by standard Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) across sparsity regimes and in some cases exceed vanilla lottery ticket accuracy at very high sparsity levels (e.g., at 96%+ sparsity on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100), indicating that training on a pruning-aware subset can preserve or improve generalization of the identified sparse model compared to full-data IMP.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 6's claim that PrAC tickets can outperform vanilla LT at high sparsity relies on small accuracy differences from three runs (P5). The statistical evidence is weak (overlapping error bars, no hypothesis test), and the phenomenon is not independently replicated. Without a highlight providing stronger statistical or mechanistic support, the outperformance claim is tentative and likely not robust. The prior probability is low because the data do not convincingly support the claim.

nodes.title: PrAC-found tickets match or can outperform vanilla IMP at high sparsity

nodes.content: A Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) set constructed using a small source network (e.g., ResNet-20) on a dataset is reusable: when transferred to larger or different architectures (e.g., ResNet-56, VGG-16) on the same dataset, the transferred PrAC set enables finding PrAC lottery tickets whose test accuracies are competitive with PrAC tickets built natively for the target architectures, demonstrating practical amortization of the PrAC-construction cost across architectures.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 7's claim of transferability across architectures is supported by highlight H2, which provides direct experimental evidence that a PrAC set from ResNet-20 transfers effectively to ResNet-56 and VGG-16 on the same dataset. However, premise P6 notes the narrow scope: only one source architecture, one direction, and no cross-dataset or cross-family validation. The highlight underwrites the claim within the tested regime, but the conclusion's generality beyond that is uncertain. The prior probability is moderate-high, reflecting strong evidence for the tested cases but limited validation for broader claims.

nodes.title: PrAC sets transfer across architectures to locate winning tickets in target models

nodes.content: Under matched computational budgets (same number of training iterations and same number of training examples), subnetworks identified by the Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) co-design pipeline outperform (a) data-selective baselines such as entropy-based active sampling and core-set selection via proxy (SVP), and (b) pruning-at-initialization methods (SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow) implemented iteratively with matched computational budgets. For example, at 93.13% sparsity on CIFAR-10, PrAC tickets outperform SynFlow by 1.51%, SNIP by 5.47%, and GraSP by 18.73% in test accuracy under matched computational conditions.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 8's claim of superiority over alternative methods is supported by highlight H3, which shows a consistent margin under matched computational budgets across multiple baselines. However, premise P7 raises concerns about the fairness of the baseline implementations: iterative use of one-shot pruning methods may not be optimal, and lack of tuning could disadvantage them. The highlight preempts the failure mode of unequal compute but not the failure mode of suboptimal baseline configuration. Thus, while the qualitative claim of superiority is likely justified, the quantitative margins are uncertain.

nodes.title: PrAC-based ticket finding outperforms alternative data selection and pruning-at-initialization baselines at equal computation

nodes.content: The Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) set decomposes into CET (Critical Examples for Training, selected by forgetting statistics) and CEP (Critical Examples for Pruning, selected by disagreement after pruning). Ablation experiments show that using CET alone yields subnetworks with an approximate ~1% test-accuracy deficit compared to the full PrAC co-design pipeline, indicating CEP contributes nontrivially. Empirically, as sparsity increases the number of CEP samples grows and the overlap fraction |CEP ∩ CET|/|CEP| decreases, indicating that pruning-sensitive examples become increasingly distinct from training-forgetting examples at higher sparsities.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 9's ablation claims are strongly supported by highlight H4, which quantifies the ~1% accuracy drop when CEP is removed and traces the increasing distinctness of CEP at higher sparsity. No weak points were identified; the ablation is thorough and the quantitative analysis is clear. The conclusion's descriptive claims about complementarity are well-grounded, and the prior probability is high.

nodes.title: Ablation: the two PrAC components (CET and CEP) have complementary roles; CEP grows with sparsity and its overlap with CET decreases

nodes.content: Visual inspection and class-wise statistics reveal that images included in Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) sets tend to be semantically more ambiguous or visually complex (e.g., multiple objects, cluttered backgrounds, lower quality), whereas excluded images are often centered, clean, and easily distinguishable. The class-wise counts within PrAC sets are approximately balanced (images per class are of the same order), indicating PrAC-construction does not produce severe class imbalance.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 10's characterization of PrAC examples as visually ambiguous yet class-balanced is based on qualitative inspection and class-ratio plots (Figure A15). No weak points or highlights were identified. The class-balance claim is supported by data, but the visual ambiguity assertion is subjective. The conclusion is not load-bearing for the main results; its credibility is moderate.

nodes.title: Characterization of PrAC examples: visually and class-wise they are more ambiguous yet balanced

nodes.content: In the Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) co-design pipeline, after a PrAC set $\mathcal{P}$ of size $|\mathcal{P}|$ is constructed from the full training dataset $\mathcal{D}_0$ of size $|\mathcal{D}_0|$, the number of training iterations $N$ for the subsequent training round of the pruned subnetwork is set to $N = (|\mathcal{P}| / |\mathcal{D}_0|) \cdot N_0$, where $N_0$ is the original number of iterations used when training on the full dataset. The pipeline does not provide a justification that the number of iterations required for the subnetwork to converge scales linearly with the fraction of data retained, nor does it empirically validate that this scaling is sufficient for the lottery ticket finding task.

metadata.failure_mode: If the linear scaling assumption is false and the required iterations do not decrease proportionally with PrAC size, then the claimed iteration savings (e.g., 83%–93% on CIFAR-10) could be overestimated. The subnetworks may be undertrained, leading to lower test accuracy that would break the claim that PrAC tickets "match" vanilla lottery ticket performance at the reported sparsity levels. The conclusion that the pipeline yields large reductions in training iterations would be invalidated because the savings figure would not correspond to a properly trained subnetwork.
metadata.weakness_reason: The linear scaling rule is introduced as an operational choice without theoretical or empirical support. In typical deep learning, the relationship between dataset size and convergence time is problem-dependent and often sub-linear, especially when the subset is not randomly drawn but selected for difficulty. The paper does not test whether halving the data halves the required iterations; it could overestimate or underestimate the needed budget, and the reported iteration savings depend directly on this untested assumption.

nodes.title: Linear scaling of training iterations with PrAC set size is unvalidated

nodes.content: In the Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) co-design pipeline, early stopping is triggered when the Hamming distance between successive binary masks of the subnetwork falls below a fixed threshold of 0.07. The justification for this threshold, its appropriateness across different architectures (e.g., ResNet-20, ResNet-56, VGG-16) and datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet), and the sensitivity of the stopping point and the accuracy-savings trade-off to small variations in the threshold are not examined.

metadata.failure_mode: If the threshold 0.07 is not appropriate for a specific configuration (e.g., the Hamming distance converges to a plateau at 0.08), then early stopping would be triggered at a point where the mask has not yet stabilized, leading to an incompletely trained subnetwork whose final accuracy is degraded. For configurations where the plateau is below 0.07 but the mask would improve with more training, early stopping might be premature, sacrificing accuracy. In either case, the conclusion that the pipeline yields "large reductions in training iterations while matching vanilla LT performance" would fail for those configurations, limiting the claimed generality.
metadata.weakness_reason: The threshold of 0.07 is selected based on visual inspection of Figure 2 for a limited set of configurations (CIFAR-10, ResNet-20). The paper does not conduct a sensitivity analysis; without evidence that the threshold is robust, the early stopping rule may stop too early (producing undertrained masks) or too late (reducing savings) when applied to other architectures or datasets. A generic fixed threshold is unlikely to be universally optimal.

nodes.title: Early stopping Hamming-distance threshold is not robustly justified

nodes.content: The Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) set sizes reported for CIFAR-10 (35.32–37.07% of the training set), CIFAR-100 (69.55–78.19%), and Tiny-ImageNet (68.23–75.10%) are obtained using a fixed forgetting threshold $\mathcal{E}_\text{F}=0$. When $\mathcal{E}_\text{F}$ is increased to 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10, the PrAC size drops from 19,748 to 10,338 examples while the test accuracy of the found subnetworks declines from 91.05% to 88.79% on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20. Thus the reported size ranges are contingent on this specific threshold and do not represent the minimal or robust data reduction achievable while maintaining performance. Table A4

metadata.failure_mode: If a practitioner applies a different E_F (e.g., 10), the data reduction would be much larger (about 10% of the training set) but at a substantial accuracy loss (>2%). The claim in conclusion 4 that PrAC sets are "substantially smaller" (35–78% of training sets) is not a robust characterization: the actual data reduction that preserves performance parity is smaller than reported when using the default threshold. The conclusion's quantitative estimates of data reduction are therefore not generalizable.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper presents the PrAC set sizes as a feature of the datasets, but they are actually functions of a hyperparameter (E_F). The choice E_F=0 is not justified as optimal or standard, and Table A4 demonstrates that different thresholds produce markedly different sizes with corresponding accuracy trade-offs. Without exploring the threshold space more thoroughly, the reported percentages cannot be interpreted as intrinsic property of the datasets or as achievable data reduction in practice.

nodes.title: PrAC set sizes depend on the forgetting threshold and are not intrinsic

nodes.content: The evaluation criterion for claiming that Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) lottery tickets match vanilla lottery ticket (LT) performance is that the PrAC test accuracy falls within one standard deviation of the vanilla LT accuracy. No justification is provided for why this criterion is appropriate for practical equivalence, nor is it tested whether stricter criteria (e.g., within 0.2% absolute accuracy) would also yield "matching" across all sparsity levels and configurations. With typical standard deviations of 0.3–0.5%, an actual accuracy deficit of up to 0.5% is accepted.

metadata.failure_mode: If the true performance difference between PrAC and vanilla LT is, say, 0.6% (one standard deviation is 0.3%), then PrAC would still be within one standard deviation of the vanilla LT mean, and the paper would claim "matching." Under a stricter criterion, this would be a mismatch. Consequently, the reported iteration savings (e.g., 83% on CIFAR-10) that are computed only for configurations satisfying the one-standard-deviation rule would not be valid for settings where a stricter equivalence is expected. The conclusion that PrAC achieves "comparable performance" is weaker than the claim of matched performance suggests.
metadata.weakness_reason: The one-standard-deviation rule is a common heuristic but is not a rigorous equivalence test. The paper does not report what fraction of runs fell within this band, nor does it provide a confidence interval for the mean difference. Without a stricter or more formal approach, the claim of matching may be overly generous: small but consistent degradation could be masked by the width of one standard deviation.

nodes.title: Matching criterion of one standard deviation is not statistically justified

nodes.content: The assertion that Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) lottery tickets can outperform vanilla lottery tickets at very high sparsity (e.g., 96.48% sparsity on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20) is based on test accuracy differences observed from three independent runs. No statistical hypothesis test is reported, and the error bars (mean ± standard deviation) overlap between the PrAC and vanilla LT curves at that sparsity point, indicating the difference may be within random variation. Fig. 3

metadata.failure_mode: If the observed accuracy difference is due to random noise, then the conclusion that PrAC tickets can outperform vanilla LT would be false. The paper's suggestion that data-level sparsity has a regularization effect would lack empirical basis. The claim of occasional outperformance would remain an anecdotal observation with low credibility, and the conclusion that PrAC tickets "can outperform" in general would be unsupported.
metadata.weakness_reason: With only three runs, the standard error of the mean is large, and the power to detect a small difference is very low. Overlapping error bars (even if the means separate slightly) suggest the observed difference is not statistically significant. The paper does not mention whether the outperformance is consistent across runs or replicable under different seeds. Without stronger evidence, the claim of outperformance is unreliable.

nodes.title: Statistical evidence for outperformance at high sparsity is weak

nodes.content: The transferability of Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) sets across architectures is demonstrated only for one source architecture (ResNet-20, a small residual network) transferring to two target architectures (ResNet-56 and VGG-16) on the same dataset (CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100), and only in the direction from smaller to larger networks. Transfer from larger to smaller networks, between different datasets, or to architectures with fundamentally different designs (e.g., networks without skip connections, transformer architectures, or very deep VGG variants) is not tested. Fig. 4

metadata.failure_mode: If transferability fails for other architectures (e.g., MobileNet, ViT) or in the reverse direction, then the practical benefit of amortizing PrAC construction cost across many models would be limited. The conclusion's claim that PrAC sets are transferable across architectures (without qualifiers) would be an overgeneralization; the evidence only supports transfer within a similar architecture family on the same dataset.
metadata.weakness_reason: The empirical coverage is narrow: only one source, two targets, same dataset. Transferability could be asymmetric: a PrAC set from a small network may be rich enough for larger ones, but the reverse may not hold, and the paper does not test the opposite direction. Additionally, the architectures tested are all from the same family (ResNet and VGG), and there is no evidence that the PrAC set's informativeness is robust to, e.g., different data augmentations, input sizes, or tasks.

nodes.title: Transferability is demonstrated only in a narrow regime

nodes.content:
For comparisons with pruning-at-initialization methods (SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow), these methods are implemented in an iterative manner (multiple train-prune cycles) using the same number of training iterations and the same number of training data as the Pruning-Aware Critical (PrAC) pipeline, but whether hyperparameters (learning rate, weight decay, pruning schedule) were tuned for each baseline is not specified, nor are implementation details such as how masks are updated across iterations or whether subnetworks are retrained from scratch each round reported. These methods were originally designed for one-shot pruning at initialization, and the iterative usage may not reflect their optimal performance. Fig. 6
      Fig. A10

metadata.failure_mode: If the baselines are not optimally implemented, their reported test accuracies may be lower than what they could achieve with proper tuning or their native one-shot protocol. Consequently, the observed performance gap (e.g., PrAC surpassing SynFlow by 1.51%, SNIP by 5.47%, GraSP by 18.73%) might be inflated, and the conclusion that PrAC outperforms these methods under equal computation would be undermined. The specific numerical margins are not reliable.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper claims a "fair comparison" by matching computational resources, but the baseline methods may be at a disadvantage because iterative retraining is not their intended use case. Lack of hyperparameter tuning could further depress their performance. Without detailed methodology, the comparison may be biased in favor of PrAC, which is intrinsically iterative. Furthermore, the advertised "matched computational budget" imposes many training iterations on methods that are designed to be one-shot, potentially masking their advantage of lower initial cost.

nodes.title: Baseline comparison may be unfair due to suboptimal implementation of pruning-at-initialization methods

nodes.content: For the PrAC co-design pipeline on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20, the pairwise Hamming distances between successive binary masks of the trained subnetwork at sparsity levels 20%, 48.80%, 73.79%, and 93.13% converge to a value below 0.07 by approximately half of the full 182 training epochs, as shown in Figure 2. This measured convergence provides an empirical basis for the early stopping rule used in the pipeline.

metadata.credit: Without this measured convergence, the early stopping rule would rest on the untested assumption that mask distances decrease monotonically and reach a stable plateau; the empirical data preempts the failure mode that early stopping is arbitrary. The layer underwritten is the justification of the early stopping mechanism — by providing a concrete observable signal (convergence of Hamming distance) that correlates with the point where masks stabilize, the efficiency gains become interpretable and less dependent on a heuristic choice. The scope of credit is partial: the convergence is demonstrated for one architecture–dataset combination, so generalization to other settings is not directly supported by this figure alone, but the measurement itself is solid for the tested case.

nodes.title: Empirical convergence of Hamming distances justifies early stopping

nodes.content: A PrAC set constructed using a ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, when transferred as the training dataset for ResNet-56 and VGG-16 (target architectures on the same dataset), produces PrAC lottery tickets whose test accuracies across sparsity levels are within one standard deviation of PrAC tickets found natively on the target architectures, as shown in Figure 4.

metadata.credit: This transfer experiment directly supports conclusion 7 by providing a concrete, quantitative demonstration that the PrAC set discovered by a small network retains its informativeness for larger networks. Without this experiment, the claim of transferability would be speculative; with it, the conclusion that PrAC sets can amortize construction cost gains empirical backing. The layer underwritten is the generalization claim: the experiment shows that the PrAC set's effectiveness is not tied to the architecture that selected it. The scope of credit is strong for the tested configurations (ResNet-20 source to ResNet-56 and VGG-16 targets on the same dataset), but limited to those conditions.

nodes.title: Direct experimental evidence of PrAC set transferability across architectures

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20, the paper evaluates PrAC lottery tickets against multiple baselines under matched computational resources: three pruning-at-initialization methods (SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow) implemented iteratively with the same number of training iterations and training data, plus two data-selection methods (Entropy-based active sampling and SVP core-set selection) and random sampling. The paper reports consistently higher test accuracies for PrAC across all sparsity levels (e.g., at 93.13% sparsity PrAC surpasses SynFlow by 1.51%, SNIP by 5.47%, GraSP by 18.73%), as shown in Figures 5, 6, and A10.

metadata.credit: This comprehensive baseline comparison preempts the failure mode that PrAC's success could be attributed to additional computation or data: by enforcing equal training iterations and training set size across all methods, the paper isolates the quality of the data subset as the source of improvement. The layer underwritten is the claim of superiority over existing efficient pruning methods; without these controls, the observed margins could be an artifact of unequal resources. The scope of credit is substantial: the comparison is consistent across multiple baselines, though the iterative implementation of one-shot methods may not fully realize their potential.

nodes.title: Comprehensive baseline comparison with matched computational budgets

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20, the paper runs the PrAC pipeline using only the CET component (forgetting-based selection) and compares to full PrAC (CET + CEP); CET-only subnetworks incur an approximate 1% test-accuracy deficit across sparsity levels (Figure A12). Additionally, Table A3 reports that as sparsity increases from 20% to 96.48%, the number of CEP samples grows from 1,501 to 6,616 and the overlap rate between CEP and CET (|CEP ∩ CET| / |CEP|) decreases from 99.40% to 82.92%, indicating that pruning-sensitive examples become increasingly distinct from training-forgetting examples.

metadata.credit: This ablation preempts the failure mode that the PrAC set's performance is driven entirely by the forgetting-based selection (CET) and that the pruning-disagreement component (CEP) is unnecessary. The quantified ~1% accuracy drop provides concrete evidence that CEP contributes, while the evolution of CEP size and overlap rate explains why its role grows at higher sparsity. The layer underwritten is the attribution of the PrAC set's effectiveness to both components; without this, the inclusion of CEP would be speculative. The scope of credit is strong for the tested setting (ResNet-20, CIFAR-10) and provides a clear mechanistic picture that supports the conclusion.

nodes.title: Ablation study isolates contributions of CET and CEP with quantitative analysis

steps.reasoning: Define the context and the objective of the selection: let $\mathcal{D}_0$ denote the full training dataset (the set of all training examples), let $f(\boldsymbol{\theta},x)$ denote the full dense model with parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ evaluated on input $x$, and let $f(\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},x)$ denote a pruned subnetwork where $\boldsymbol{m}\in\{0,1\}^{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_0}$ is a binary mask and $\odot$ is element-wise multiplication; the goal is to construct a compact subset $\mathcal{P}\subset\mathcal{D}_0$ that captures examples which are both (a) difficult to learn during network training and (b) fragile to pruning-induced changes in the model, so that $\mathcal{P}$ supports locating trainable sparse subnetworks.

Motivate why both types of examples are needed: training-difficulty (hard-to-memorize) examples capture dense-model generalization difficulty, while pruning-fragile (easy-to-forget-after-pruning) examples capture sensitivity introduced by model sparsification; omitting either kind risks losing signals required to identify sparse, trainable connectivity patterns (this motivation is stated as the escalation from standard "coreset" requirements to the higher bar needed for lottery-ticket discovery).

Introduce the first concrete selection criterion, the "forgetting statistics" per sample, and define the metric precisely: for a given sample $x\in\mathcal{D}_0$, its forgetting statistic is the number-of-transitions-from-correct-to-incorrect over the course of training (i.e., each time the sample moves from being correctly classified to incorrectly classified increments the count); denote the forgetting count of $x$ by $\text{forget}(x)$. A threshold $\mathcal{E}_\text{F}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ is chosen, and any sample with $\text{forget}(x)>\mathcal{E}_\text{F}$ is considered "hard-to-memorize" and is selected into the set of Critical Examples for Training (CET).
(Toneva et al., 2019)

Introduce the second concrete selection criterion, the pruning-disagreement test, and define it precisely: for each sample $x\in\mathcal{D}_0$, compute the predicted class of the full dense model $f(\boldsymbol{\theta},x)$ and of the pruned subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},x)$; denote the predicted classes by $\hat{y}_\text{full}(x)$ and $\hat{y}_\text{pruned}(x)$ respectively. If $\hat{y}_\text{full}(x) \neq \hat{y}_\text{pruned}(x)$, then $x$ is classified as "easy-to-forget-by-pruning" and is selected into the set of Critical Examples for Pruning (CEP). This criterion operationalizes pruning-induced fragility by explicit prediction disagreement between dense and pruned models.
(Hooker et al., 2020a)

Define the Pruning-Aware Critical set (PrAC set) and its construction rule precisely: the PrAC set $\mathcal{P}$ is the union of the CET and CEP selections, i.e., $\mathcal{P} = \{x\in\mathcal{D}_0 : \text{forget}(x)>\mathcal{E}_\text{F}\} \;\cup\; \{x\in\mathcal{D}_0 : \hat{y}_\text{full}(x)\neq\hat{y}_\text{pruned}(x)\}$. This union is intended to encode both dense-model generalization difficulty (via forgetting) and pruning-induced fragility (via disagreement).

Tie the concrete selection steps to the iterative construction loop: during an iteration where a current mask $\boldsymbol{m}$ and a training set $\mathcal{D}$ are available, first compute forgetting statistics for all $x\in\mathcal{D}$ by training the current subnetwork and recording transitions (as in the forgetting statistic definition) and add those with $\text{forget}(x)>\mathcal{E}_\text{F}$ into $\mathcal{P}$; then, after pruning and obtaining an updated mask $\boldsymbol{m}$, evaluate $\hat{y}_\text{full}(x)$ and $\hat{y}_\text{pruned}(x)$ for $x\in\mathcal{D}_0$ and add disagreement examples into $\mathcal{P}$; finally set the next iteration's dataset $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{P}$. These procedural steps are the operational instantiation of the two criteria within the iterative algorithm.

State the intended effect of this design: by explicitly selecting samples that are either repeatedly forgotten during training or on which pruning changes predicted labels, the constructed PrAC set retains examples that are hypothesized to determine both dense-model generalization difficulty and sparse-model trainability, thereby enabling reduced-data iterations that still preserve the signals required to locate winning tickets.

State the starting point (use upstream conclusion as given): the PrAC set construction rule (select CET via forgetting statistics and CEP via full-vs-pruned prediction disagreement) is available and will be embedded inside an iterative data-model co-design loop to locate sparse masks.

Define initial symbols and initialization for the pipeline: let $\mathcal{D}_0$ denote the full training set, let $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ denote the initial weights of the dense network, let $\boldsymbol{m}\in\{0,1\}^{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\|_0}$ denote the binary sparsity mask, let $s\in[0,1]$ denote the desired overall sparsity fraction (fraction of weights to be zeroed), let $\rho\in[0,1]$ denote the per-iteration pruning fraction (the fraction of remaining nonzero weights to prune at each pruning step), let $T$ denote the number of training epochs used to collect forgetting statistics within an iteration, and let $\mathcal{D}$ denote the current training dataset used in that iteration; initialize $\boldsymbol{m}=\mathbf{1}$ (all-ones mask, i.e., no pruning yet) and $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_0$.

Describe the outer loop termination condition precisely: iterate the following body while the current sparsity level is less than the desired sparsity $s$, i.e., while $1 - \frac{\|\boldsymbol{m}\|_0}{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\|_0} \le s$ (where $\|\cdot\|_0$ denotes the number of nonzero entries).

Detail the data-slimming substep that constructs CET within each iteration: set $\mathcal{P}=\varnothing$ initially; train the current subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_0,\cdot)$ on $\mathcal{D}$ for $T$ epochs while updating forgetting statistics for all samples $x\in\mathcal{D}$ (i.e., counting transitions correct→incorrect); select all samples with forgetting count $>\mathcal{E}_\text{F}$ and add them to $\mathcal{P}$ (this operationalizes the CET selection criterion from the PrAC definition).

Detail the model-slimming (pruning) substep within each iteration: after the training in the iteration, take the trained subnetwork parameters (denote the trained parameters by $\boldsymbol{\theta}_T$) and prune a fraction $\rho$ (the implementation uses $\rho=20\%$ as a default) of the remaining nonzero weights of $f(\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_T,\cdot)$ according to magnitude (iterative magnitude pruning), and update the binary mask $\boldsymbol{m}$ accordingly to reflect the newly pruned weights.
(Han et al., 2015)

Detail the pruning-disagreement substep that constructs CEP within each iteration: for samples $x\in\mathcal{D}_0$ evaluate the predicted class of the full dense model $f(\boldsymbol{\theta},x)$ (where $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ denotes the current full model parameters) and the pruned subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},x)$; for any $x$ with differing predicted classes, add $x$ to $\mathcal{P}$ (this operationalizes the CEP selection criterion from the PrAC definition).

Update the dataset for the next iteration precisely: after CET and CEP additions, set $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{P}$ so the next iteration trains on the newly constructed PrAC set; then repeat the loop until the desired overall sparsity $s$ is reached. The final outputs are the sparse mask $\boldsymbol{m}$ and its associated PrAC set $\mathcal{P}$.

Explain why this co-design addresses the computational bottleneck of conventional IMP: conventional Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) requires repeated full-data training and pruning cycles which are computationally expensive; by replacing the full-data training at each pruning iteration with training on an iteratively constructed, much smaller PrAC subset that explicitly preserves pruning-sensitive examples, the per-epoch cost is reduced and the dataset evolves jointly with the mask to retain signals necessary to locate trainable sparse masks, thereby reducing the total computational burden of the train-prune-retrain process.
(Frankle & Carbin, 2018)

State the starting point (upstream conclusion used): the iterative co-design pipeline that constructs and uses PrAC sets inside an IMP-style loop is established and available as the operational context for efficiency techniques.

Define the symbols and the dynamic-iteration-scaling formula precisely: let $N_0$ denote the original number of training iterations used when training on the full dataset $\mathcal{D}_0$, let $|\mathcal{D}_0|$ denote the cardinality (size) of the full training set, and let $|\mathcal{P}|$ denote the size of the constructed PrAC set. The dynamic training-iteration scaling rule sets the adjusted number of iterations $N$ to
$N = \frac{|\mathcal{P}|}{|\mathcal{D}_0|} N_0$,
i.e., training iterations are scaled linearly in proportion to the reduced dataset size. The learning-rate schedule is also re-calculated accordingly using the same proportional adjustment.

Explain the rationale behind proportional scaling: reducing the number of training examples reduces per-epoch computation, but additional speedups come from the expectation that a smaller, easier-to-fit dataset will converge in fewer epochs; therefore a simple proportional reduction of total iterations is used as a first-principles adjustment to realize non-linear gains in total training effort when combined with other early termination criteria.

Define the early-stopping mechanism and the Hamming-distance monitoring precisely: after each training epoch compute the current binary sparsity mask $\boldsymbol{m}^{(t)}$ (where $t$ indexes epochs within the iteration). Define the Hamming distance between two masks as the number of differing entries: for masks $\boldsymbol{m}^{(t)}$ and $\boldsymbol{m}^{(t')}$ the Hamming distance is $\text{Ham}(\boldsymbol{m}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{m}^{(t')}) = |\{i: m^{(t)}_i \neq m^{(t')}_i\}|$. Use the Hamming-distance between successive masks as the convergence monitor and interrupt training early when the Hamming distance falls below a threshold (the implementation uses a default threshold of $0.07$).

Connect this early-stopping mechanism to prior empirical observations and justify its use: the early-bird ticket observation (that stable sparsity masks emerge early in training) supports using mask-convergence as a stopping rule; therefore monitoring Hamming distances and stopping when they converge is expected to permit safely interrupting training and proceeding to pruning while preserving the mask-identification quality.
(You et al., 2020)

Report the empirical validation of mask-convergence and the chosen Hamming threshold: the Hamming distances between masks were empirically observed to converge early in training (around half of the full training schedule), as shown by the plotted pairwise Hamming-distance trajectories; this empirical behavior validates the early-stopping mechanism and motivates the default Hamming-threshold of $0.07$ used to interrupt training and proceed to pruning.
Fig. 2

Start from the pipeline being available (upstream conclusion used): the iterative co-design pipeline that constructs PrAC sets during iterative pruning is in place and is the mechanism by which PrAC sizes are empirically measured.

State the datasets and networks for which PrAC sizes were measured: CIFAR-10 (10 classes), CIFAR-100 (100 classes), and Tiny-ImageNet (200 classes) with architectures including ResNet-20, ResNet-56, ResNet-18, and VGG-16; these are the experimental settings used to quantify achievable data reduction.

Report the measured PrAC set-size proportions precisely (empirical results reproduced from the experiments table): on CIFAR-10 the PrAC sets ranged from $35.32\%$ to $37.07\%$ of the full training set across considered architectures; on CIFAR-100 the PrAC sets ranged from $69.55\%$ to $78.19\%$; on Tiny-ImageNet the PrAC sets ranged from $68.23\%$ to $75.10\%$. These ranges provide concrete empirical bounds on how compact pruning-aware subsets can be while still supporting winning-ticket discovery in the evaluated settings.
Table A2

Explain the interpretation given by the authors: these empirical PrAC-size ranges show that achievable data reduction varies with task complexity (fewer classes allow smaller PrAC sets) and that PrAC sizes are substantially smaller than full training sets on CIFAR-10 in particular, quantifying the practical data-level savings possible when co-designing data and model sparsity for lottery-ticket finding.

Begin from upstream conclusions used as known: the iterative co-design pipeline (conclusion 2) and the efficiency techniques of dynamic iteration scaling and early stopping (conclusion 3) are available as the operational framework for measuring iteration savings.

Define the metric being reported and the matching criterion: the total training iterations used to find a matching subnetwork (a subnetwork that reaches performance comparable to vanilla IMP-found winning tickets) are recorded for both PrAC-driven runs and vanilla full-data IMP runs; the authors consider PrAC lottery tickets to achieve matched performance when the PrAC ticket's test accuracy is within one standard deviation of the vanilla lottery ticket's test accuracy at the same sparsity.
Fig. 3

Report the empirical iteration-savings numbers precisely as measured across datasets and architectures: on CIFAR-10 the PrAC pipeline achieves training-iteration savings in the range $82.85\%\!-\!92.77\%$ across architectures; on CIFAR-100 the savings range $63.54\%\!-\!74.92\%$; on Tiny-ImageNet the savings range $76.14\%\!-\!86.56\%$. These percentages are computed by comparing the total iterations needed by the PrAC pipeline (with dynamic scaling and early stopping) to the iterations used by vanilla IMP to reach comparable subnetwork performance.
Fig. 3

Explain how the efficiency techniques contribute to these reductions: reductions in dataset size reduce per-epoch compute linearly, the dynamic iteration scaling reduces the total number of iterations $N$ proportionally to $|\mathcal{P}|/|\mathcal{D}_0|$, and the Hamming-distance early stopping further truncates training epochs when mask convergence is detected; together these mechanisms produce the observed large, non-linear reductions in total training iterations required to find matching subnetworks.

State the maintained performance outcome: despite the reduced iterations, the subnetworks found via the PrAC pipeline match the test accuracies of subnetworks identified by standard full-data IMP (vanilla lottery ticket) procedures in the evaluated settings, supporting the claim that substantial iteration savings can be realized while preserving final sparse-subnetwork accuracy.
Fig. 3

Start from upstream conclusion used as known: the co-design pipeline that constructs PrAC sets and uses dynamic scaling and early stopping (conclusions 2 and 3) is in place and its empirical evaluation produces accuracy curves and iteration counts.

Report the empirical parity and occasional improvement precisely: across the evaluated sparsity regimes, PrAC-found subnetworks ("PrAC lottery tickets") achieve test accuracies that are statistically indistinguishable from vanilla IMP-found winning tickets (i.e., within the same mean and standard-deviation ranges reported), and at very high sparsity (for example, at $\sim\!96\%$ sparsity on CIFAR variants) PrAC tickets can exceed vanilla-LT accuracy; these behaviors are visible in the plotted test-accuracy vs. sparsity curves and associated reported points.
Fig. 3
Fig. 6

Reproduce the authors' concrete illustrative observation: the paper highlights that at the highest sparsity of 96.48% on some CIFAR experiments the PrAC-found ticket outperforms the vanilla ticket (this specific numerical example is reported in the visual summary and discussed as an instance of PrAC sometimes exceeding vanilla-LT performance).
Fig. 1

Explain the tentative interpretation and note the lack of theoretical derivation: the authors conjecture that training on a pruning-aware reduced dataset can have a regularization-like effect that occasionally improves the generalization of extremely sparse subnetworks, but explicitly state that the mechanism is not theoretically explained in the paper and is left for future investigation (i.e., the empirical improvement is reported without a derived cause).

Begin from upstream conclusion used as known: the iterative co-design pipeline (conclusion 2) is used to construct PrAC sets, and this enables evaluating whether a PrAC set built with one (source) architecture can be reused to find tickets in other (target) architectures on the same dataset.

Describe the transfer experiment protocol precisely: construct a PrAC set using a small source network (the paper uses ResNet-20 as the source architecture) on a dataset (CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100); then, for each target architecture (for example, ResNet-56 and VGG-16), locate sparse subnetworks using the transferred PrAC set (i.e., train-prune-retrain the target architecture using the same PrAC samples and the pipeline machinery) and compare the test accuracies of PrAC tickets found using the transferred PrAC set against PrAC tickets constructed natively for the target architecture.

Report the empirical transfer result and its interpretation: the transferred PrAC sets enable finding subnetworks whose test accuracies are competitive with those of PrAC tickets built natively for the target architectures (the plotted accuracy-vs-sparsity curves for transferred and native PrAC tickets are similar across most sparsity levels), showing that PrAC sets are reusable across architectures and thus can amortize the cost of constructing PrAC sets in practice.
Fig. 4

State the practical implication emphasized by the authors: because constructing a PrAC set has an upfront cost, the ability to reuse a PrAC set found with a small/cheap architecture to locate tickets in larger/expensive architectures reduces the per-target overhead and makes the overall approach practically attractive for large-model settings.

Start from the pipeline being available (upstream conclusion used): with the PrAC co-design pipeline (conclusion 2) one can compare PrAC-driven ticket finding to alternative data-selection and pruning-at-initialization baselines under matched computational budgets.

Define the fairness condition used in comparisons: comparisons are run under matched computational budgets, meaning each method is given the same number of training iterations and the same number of training examples (so that any performance gap is due to the method rather than extra computation or data).

List the baselines compared and how they were adapted for fairness: (a) data-selective baselines including entropy-based active sampling ("Entropy") and core-set proxy selection ("SVP") are given the same number of examples and iterations; (b) pruning-at-initialization and single-shot methods (SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow) are implemented iteratively (iterating their one-shot criteria multiple times) so their total training iterations and training-data consumption match the PrAC pipeline; random sampling is included as a sanity check.

Report the empirical superiority and a concrete numerical example: PrAC-identified subnetworks outperform the listed baselines under matched computational budgets across sparsity regimes; for example, at 93.13% sparsity on CIFAR-10, PrAC tickets outperform SynFlow by $1.51\%$ test accuracy, SNIP by $5.47\%$, and GraSP by $18.73\%$, demonstrating that the gains arise from the pruning-aware data selection rather than extra computation.
Fig. 5
Fig. 6

Explain the authors' interpretation of the result: because all methods were constrained to equal computation and data budgets, the observed performance gap verifies that co-designing the dataset to preserve both forgetting and pruning-disagreement examples produces more informative, pruning-aware subsets that help locate higher-quality winning tickets than either generic coresets/active sampling or pruning-at-initialization heuristics iterated to parity.
Fig. A10

Start from the pipeline being available (upstream conclusion used): the PrAC set is defined as the union of CET (Critical Examples for Training) and CEP (Critical Examples for Pruning); an ablation can therefore compare using CET alone vs. the full union to determine the contribution of CEP.

Define CET and CEP precisely for the ablation context: CET is the set of training samples selected solely by the forgetting-statistic thresholding rule ($\text{forget}(x)>\mathcal{E}_\text{F}$); CEP is the set of samples selected solely by prediction disagreement between the full and pruned models ($\hat{y}_\text{full}(x)\neq\hat{y}_\text{pruned}(x)$). The PrAC set is $\text{PrAC} = \text{CET} \cup \text{CEP}$.

Report the CET-only performance deficit precisely as observed: ablation experiments that use CET alone to identify subnetworks yield subnetworks that incur an approximate $\sim 1\%$ test-accuracy deficit relative to subnetworks found using the full PrAC pipeline (i.e., CET∪CEP). This indicates that CEP contributes nontrivially to preserving final accuracy and that training-difficulty signals alone do not fully capture pruning fragility.
Fig. A12

Report the empirical trends of CEP size and overlap with CET as sparsity increases, reproducing the observed statistics: Table A3 reports the counts of CEP, CET, and PrAC at multiple sparsity levels and the overlapping rate defined as $|CEP\cap CET|/|CEP|$; as sparsity increases, the number of CEP samples grows (numerical entries in Table A3 show CEP increasing from thousands to over six thousand at higher sparsities), while the overlap fraction $|CEP\cap CET|/|CEP|$ generally decreases (Table A3 shows the overlapping rate falling from $\sim99.40\%$ at low sparsity to values in the $77\%\!-\!83\%$ range at very high sparsities), indicating CEP becomes increasingly distinct from CET at higher sparsities.
Table A3

Summarize the complementary-role conclusion: together these observations show that CET and CEP play complementary roles in PrAC construction—CET captures training-difficulty signals but CEP captures pruning-sensitive examples that grow in importance as the network becomes sparser—and therefore the union is necessary to best preserve sparse-model trainability across sparsity regimes.

Start from the pipeline being available (upstream conclusion used): with PrAC sets constructed, the authors inspect the contents of PrAC sets both visually and via class-wise counts to characterize what types of images survive the pruning-aware selection.

Describe the visual-inspection findings and give concrete qualitative contrasts: images excluded from the PrAC set tend to be centered, high-quality, and easily distinguishable single-object images (for example, an orange centered on a white background), whereas images included in the PrAC set tend to be semantically more ambiguous or visually complex — examples include lower-quality images, images that depict multiple objects, cluttered backgrounds, or other factors that make recognition challenging even for a human; these qualitative observations are illustrated by side-by-side visualizations of images outside and inside the final PrAC set.
Fig. 9

Describe the class-wise-count findings and define the measure: the per-class counts within the PrAC sets are examined and reported as class-wise ratios (counts of images per class in the PrAC set); these counts are observed to be approximately balanced, i.e., the numbers of images from different classes are of the same order and no severe class imbalance is induced by PrAC construction.
Fig. A15

Explain the interpretation the authors draw from these characterizations: the fact that PrAC retains harder, ambiguous examples while remaining class-balanced supports the hypothesis that PrAC preserves informative inputs that determine sparse-model behavior, and helps explain empirically why PrAC-found tickets generalize and match full-data IMP performance rather than succeeding due to a trivial or biased subset.

open_questions.content: Several scientifically meaningful issues remain open as acknowledged by the work. First, the mechanism by which training on a pruning-aware, reduced dataset can sometimes improve generalization of extremely sparse subnetworks is not theoretically explained and is left for future investigation; the paper notes this empirical regularization-like effect without deriving its cause. Second, practical deployment requires quantifying the cost-benefit tradeoff of constructing a PrAC set versus the amortized savings when transferring a PrAC across many target models; the paper demonstrates transferability but does not provide a formal analysis of when the initial PrAC construction cost is justified for very large target models or datasets. Third, the method relies on hyperparameters (the forgetting threshold $\mathcal{E}_\text{F}$, the per-epoch training budget $T$ for collecting forgetting statistics, and the Hamming-distance threshold for early stopping); choosing these values affects PrAC size and final accuracy (Table A4 shows performance varies with $\mathcal{E}_\text{F}$), and optimal, generally-applicable setting or adaptive selection strategies remain unresolved. Finally, the evaluation is restricted to image-classification benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet) and ResNet/VGG families; whether the PrAC co-design generalizes across different modalities, tasks (e.g., detection, segmentation, language), and larger-scale datasets is not addressed and is an explicit direction for future work.
